lesson.title: One Pool, One Coin Flip: The Completely Randomized Design
lesson.summary: In a completely randomized design, every experimental unit is drawn from a single pool and assigned to a treatment purely by chance, with no grouping or blocking applied before randomization.
lesson.body:
A completely randomized design is the simplest and most direct way to run an experiment. Every experimental unit, whether it is a person, a plant, or a manufactured part, is treated as belonging to one single pool. From that pool, units are assigned to treatments entirely by chance, using the kind of random assignment procedure discussed earlier, with no additional structure imposed beforehand. There is no sorting by age, sex, location, or any other characteristic before the randomization happens; the randomization itself is expected to do all of the balancing work.

It helps to see what this looks like in practice. Suppose an agricultural researcher wants to compare three fertilizers, call them A, B, and C, on tomato yield, using 60 tomato plants in a greenhouse. In a completely randomized design, she does not separate the plants by shelf, by pot size, or by how much sunlight each spot receives. Instead she numbers all 60 plants 01 through 60 and uses a random number generator to assign exactly 20 plants to fertilizer A, 20 to fertilizer B, and 20 to fertilizer C, drawing from the full list of 60 in one single randomization step. Every plant, regardless of its shelf or pot, has the same chance of landing in any of the three groups.

The appeal of this design is its simplicity: it is easy to carry out, easy to explain, and easy to analyze statistically because the three groups were formed by one uniform chance process. It works especially well when the experimental units are fairly similar to each other to begin with, so there is no obvious variable like plant age or original pot size that the researcher already suspects will affect the outcome. When such a known source of variability does exist, a completely randomized design can still be valid, but it may waste some precision, since the shelf-to-shelf differences in light get mixed randomly into all three groups rather than being controlled for directly, which is one reason statisticians sometimes prefer a randomized block design instead.

A completely randomized design can also include a control group that receives no treatment, or a placebo, alongside the active treatments, as long as membership in every group, including the control, is decided by the same single randomization. For example, if the tomato study had included a fourth group of 20 plants that received no fertilizer at all as a baseline, that group would simply be one more category assigned by the identical chance procedure, not something singled out for special treatment in how it was formed.

Because every unit in a completely randomized design has an equal, known chance of ending up in any treatment group, and because that assignment happens independently of any of the unit's own characteristics, this design is what allows the researcher to attach a legitimate margin of error and significance test to the comparison between groups afterward. Without that one unifying random assignment step tying every unit together, the statistical machinery used to compare group means, such as a two sample t-test or one-way ANOVA, would not have a solid probabilistic foundation to stand on.
